e: Borrowed from Iranian Persian تَعْزِیِه (ta'ziye), from Classical Persian تَعْزِیَه (ta'ziya), from Arabic تَعْزِيَة (taʕziya, “condolence”).
Imitative, supposed to represent a fanfare. First attested in the 1920s.
q: "I give you the Illusion of the Reborn Hand. Ta-daaa!"
1978, Barry B. Longyear, Circus World, published 1982, page 94:
“[…]Well, ta-ta, sweetheart! Don′t expect me back to lunch.”
1917, Henry Handel Richardson, Australia Felix, The Echo Library, published 2007, page 229:
‘No more questions? Then I′ll be off. Ta-ta.’

e:
Uncertain, but possibly young child's pronunciation of thanks.
Alternatively, derived from Danish tak, from Old Norse þǫkk, from Proto-Germanic *þankō, *þankaz.
Altered from si in the 19th century to prevent having two notes of the musical scale starting with the same letter, to become ti. vowel changed to 'a' to signify a flattened note.
q: Go on, break out a "how's yew 'uns doin'? Right pleasure ta meet yew ’uns"!
